items.title: Dawoud Sabu Adeyola interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 30, 2025
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] You made me think of Joe Williams performed here and he introduced one song and he said, “Blues frees the spirit.” [INTERVIEWEE] Yeah, yeah. It does, it does.

ctx.x: any of the literary things and so we do a careful analysis of the musical history whether it be blues, whether it be folk, or gospel or church music or whatnot, we can get a good idea of what was going on in terms of civil rights, in terms of human rights and human suffering and degradation. You can hear the cries in the music. And so that’s why I really think that the Lord Almighty gave us the blues, which seems it’s not going to ever go away you know and it has many forms. I mean almost all American music forms…
You made me think of Joe Williams performed here and he introduced one song and he said, “Blues frees the spirit.”

Yeah, yeah. It does, it does. And it really comes out of the old spirituals when people were singing and hopes for and prayers for a better day, better conditions. I saw a heart wrenching interview, I mean sometimes stuff just pops up on YouTube and I say, “Oh I’ve just got to hear this,” something popped up the other day, somebody interviewed Nina Simone after she had left the States and went to France I think when she came back and they were interviewing her. And they asked her, you know, “Why did you leave?”…
